title: Voyager 1 Reaches a Light-Day From Earth, Nearly a Decade Before Its Twin
summary:
On November 18, Voyager 1 will be so far from Earth that a radio signal will take a full day, 24 hours, to reach it. That distance is called a light-day: about 16,094,799,096 miles from home. NASA is celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse code signals at the sky. Its twin, Voyager 2, will not reach the same mark until about 2035, nearly a decade later.

The gap comes down to choices made for speed and science while the spacecraft were flying by planets. Voyager 2 launched first in 1977, with Voyager 1 following about two weeks later on a faster path. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979, while Voyager 2 got there four months later, on July 9.

Each spacecraft then used a gravity assist, a slingshot around a planet that borrows a tiny bit of the planet's momentum to gain speed while saving fuel. Each Voyager gained about 10 kilometers per second at Jupiter, and the planets themselves did not slow down by any measurable amount. The two spacecraft were both aimed at Jupiter and Saturn at first, but their paths then split.

Voyager 1 turned at Saturn to study the planet's rings and its moon Titan before flying out of the plane of the solar system. Voyager 2 kept going to Uranus and Neptune on a rare planetary alignment, but it lost about 2 kilometers per second at Neptune when it turned to fly by Triton.

Today Voyager 1 is zooming outward at 3.5 Earth-sun distances a year, while Voyager 2 travels at a more stately 3.1. Both have now left the solar system, Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018, and they could keep working into the 2030s while their nuclear power lasts.
why_it_matters: The Voyagers are the farthest human-made objects ever sent into space, and their long journeys show how small choices in a flight path can shape decades of exploration.
